name: Portulaca oleracea
lead: Portulaca oleracea, commonly purslane, is a warm-climate succulent annual eaten as a leafy vegetable in the Mediterranean, Middle East, Asia and Mexico and used in folk medicine in many countries.[1][2] In skincare, extracts appear in soothing and moisturising products; one DailyMed-listed essence combines Portulaca oleracea extract with niacinamide, glycerin and lotus flower extract.[3]

Laboratory research describes anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and wound-healing activity. A 2015 review catalogued its flavonoids, alkaloids and fatty acids and their reported pharmacological effects, and a mouse study reported faster excision-wound closure with a crude topical preparation.[4][5] No controlled clinical trial of topical purslane for skin appearance was found.

paras: The plant is a prostrate, fleshy herb with reddish stems and small yellow flowers, and is a weed in many regions. Its leaves are rich in alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid, and in vitamin E, but are also very high in oxalates.[1][6]

Traditional medicine has used purslane as an anti-inflammatory, diuretic and for burns and fevers, and Chinese tradition calls it a vegetable for long life.[2][4] In cosmetics it is promoted as a soothing botanical.[3]

A review of its phytochemistry and pharmacology summarised reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, wound-healing and other effects, mostly from cell and animal work.[4] A 2000 study reported analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects in animals, and a 2003 study in mice reported that a crude extract accelerated wound contraction.[5][7] A study of wild Nepalese vegetables measured antioxidant capacity of purslane extracts in chemical assays.[8]

Purslane is high in oxalates, which is relevant to dietary intake.[1] The product label for the essence advises external use only, avoiding broken or irritated skin, and stopping use if irritation or rash occurs.[3]

No clinical studies of purslane for skin appearance were found. A registered phase 2 trial examined purslane for oral lichen planus, and another registered study of an eyelash serum listed purslane among its ingredients.[9][10] Published results are not part of the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Edible succulent weed used as a soothing skincare botanical, backed by lab and animal data but no skin-appearance trials.
card.note: Evidence is from lab and animal studies; no topical human appearance trials found.

quick.overview:
Purslane is a common edible succulent used in folk medicine, now added to K-beauty-style soothing products.

Research reports anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects in cells and animals. No clinical trials of topical use for appearance were found.
quick.mechanism: Flavonoids, alkaloids and fatty acids in the plant show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory assays.
quick.risks: Leaves are high in oxalates when eaten. Topical product labels advise avoiding broken skin and stopping use if irritation occurs.
